data.title: Accessibility
data.tagline: Accessibility means more people can use your page in more situations—not only with a mouse, not only with perfect vision, and even read aloud by a screen reader.
data.learningOutcome: You can have the AI self-check against the three high-frequency accessibility checks, and tell them apart from "the page looks fine."
data.description: You test with a mouse and good eyes, but visitors may use a keyboard, a screen reader, or squint at a phone in sunlight. Accessibility extends "works for me" to those situations: text alternatives on images, buttons reachable by Tab, sufficient text contrast. When an AI reply mentions a11y, it is the shorthand for this word (a plus 11 letters plus y).

learning.assumes: You have used the Tab key and seen the text shown when an image fails to load.
learning.outcome: You can have the AI self-check against the three high-frequency accessibility checks, and tell them apart from "the page looks fine."

distinctions.label: Contrast
distinctions.explanation: Contrast is one specific check—text versus background; Accessibility is the whole effort that check belongs to.

distinctions.label: Focus
distinctions.explanation: Focus shows where the keyboard cursor is; Accessibility requires it be visible and reachable on every control.

explanation.title: Images have text alternatives
explanation.text: Every informative image carries alt text that steps in when the image fails or a reader reads aloud. Purely decorative icons can go without it—just do not skip images with content.

explanation.title: Keyboard can reach
explanation.text: Unplug the mouse and Tab through: every button reachable, focus visible (the focus ring), order sensible. Menus and dialogs take focus in and return it on close.

explanation.title: Contrast suffices
explanation.text: Body versus background at least 4.5:1. This one also helps everyone squinting at a phone in the sun—good accessibility benefits ordinary users too.

data.boundary: Accessibility is not only "helping people with disabilities"—sunlight glare, holding a baby with one hand, or a broken mouse all fall inside it, and everyone benefits. It is also not a post-launch patch: doing these checks during the build is straightforward; auditing every page after launch takes far more time. The a11y shorthand common in AI replies refers to exactly this.

lessonPractice.title: The AI delivered the page and you want to verify the accessibility floor. Which combination covers the most common problems?

options.label: Images have text alternatives, buttons reachable by Tab, text contrast sufficient
options.feedback: Correct. Each of the three blocks one common barrier, and together they are together they catch the most common problems in one pass.

options.label: Contrast is checked, so the page should be fine
options.feedback: Contrast covers only "hard to see"; keyboard and screen-reader users may still be locked out.

options.label: Just click through it in Chrome on your own computer
options.feedback: Same device, same browser is exactly the "works for me" trap; accessibility needs different inputs and contexts.

data.agentPrompt: Run an accessibility self-check before delivery: every image has alt text, all buttons and links are reachable by Tab in order, and body contrast is at least 4.5:1. Fix what fails and list the fixes.
